title: Building a Personal Protocol
hook: A protocol you don't use under pressure is a document, not a skill; the work is wiring it to the moments that need it.
why:
At the end of Part I you wrote a protocol: six steps, from reading yourself first to recording and revising. You may know it by heart. And at some point since, in an argument, a tense meeting or a phone call that went wrong, you will have done none of it. You read the other person in a flash, felt certain, and acted, and only afterwards remembered that you own a method for exactly that moment.

That gap is not a failure of knowledge. It is how people work under pressure, and there is good research on closing it. This chapter does not add new steps. It is about making the steps you have run when they are needed: tying them to specific triggers, compressing them into a form that survives stress, building a full and a short version, adapting them to the different parts of your life, and improving them from your own records rather than from enthusiasm. The test of a protocol is not how good it looks in your journal. It is whether it fired the last time you needed it.

teach.h: A document is not a skill.
teach.p:
Under pressure, behaviour slides back towards habit. In 2009 Lars Schwabe and Oliver Wolf trained people to win rewards by pressing keys, then changed the value of the rewards so that the old responses no longer made sense. People who had first been put through a stressful task, holding a hand in ice water while being watched and filmed, kept making the old, now pointless responses more than those who had not. Stress shifted them from acting on goals towards acting on habit.

The finding fits ordinary experience. A man who has decided to stay calm with his teenage son finds himself shouting the same sentences his own father shouted. A manager who believes in asking before assuming hears himself announce a verdict on a colleague's attitude. In both cases the better plan existed. It was simply not the strongest habit in the moment, and stress gave the moment to the strongest habit.

This is why a protocol written in a journal is only a start. Knowing the six steps is necessary and is not enough, because the moments that most need them are the moments when deliberate thought is least available. The protocol has to become the habit, or at least be tied so firmly to the situation that it fires before the old habit does.

Three things make that possible, and the rest of this chapter takes them in turn: specific plans tied to specific triggers, a form of the protocol short enough to run under load, and rehearsal in conditions close enough to the real ones that the plan has been used before it is needed.

Begin by assuming that whatever you have not practised under pressure, you will not do under pressure.
teach.disconfirm: If you find that you already run your protocol reliably in tense moments without any of the work in this chapter, your habits and your plan have already merged. Check it against the journal entries from your three hardest conversations this month.
teach.pullQuote: Whatever you have not practised under pressure, you will not do under pressure.

teach.p:
The psychologist Peter Gollwitzer distinguished between goals and what he called implementation intentions. A goal says what you want: *I will read people more carefully*. An implementation intention says when, where and how, in the form of a plan that links a specific situation to a specific response: *If a meeting turns to money, then I check my own shoulders before I look at anyone else.*

The difference is large. In 2006 Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran combined ninety-four tests of implementation intentions across health, study, work and personal goals, and found a medium-to-large effect on whether people actually did what they intended. The proposed mechanism is that the plan hands control of the response to the situation. You no longer have to remember the goal and decide to act on it in the moment. The cue itself calls up the response, much as a habit would.

For a reader of people, the most useful if-then plans attach to the moments where readings go wrong. *If I feel sudden certainty about what someone is thinking, then I name one rival explanation before I speak.* *If someone I manage goes quiet, then I ask about the situation, not the signal.* *If I am tired and the conversation matters, then I say less and ask more.*

Keep each plan to one specific situation and one specific response, small enough to do in a few seconds. A plan with two responses tends to produce neither. Write no more than three or four, because each one needs practice to stick.

And write them in your own words. A plan phrased the way you think is one your mind will find when it needs it.
teach.disconfirm: If, after a month, your if-then plans fire no more often than your general intentions did before you wrote them, they are too vague or tied to cues that do not occur. Rewrite one with a more specific trigger and track it for a fortnight.

teach.p:
An if-then plan is only as good as its *if*. A trigger has to be something that reliably happens, that you will notice when it happens, and that arrives early enough for the response to matter.

There are four useful kinds. Places and thresholds: walking through a door, sitting down at a table, picking up the phone. They are reliable and easy to notice, which makes them good for the self-check at the start of the protocol. Social moments: a question put to you, a change of subject, someone raising their voice. Times: the first five minutes of any meeting, Friday afternoon, the hour after you get home. And internal signals: the jolt of certainty, heat in your face, your jaw setting, the urge to interrupt.

The internal signals are the most important and the hardest. They are the moments at which a reading is about to turn into an action, and they come before you know you are in trouble. They are also personal. One man's warning sign is a tightening behind the eyes; another's is the sudden wish to be clever. The journal is how you find yours. Look back at the entries where you misread someone and acted on it, and note what you felt just before.

Link the internal trigger to a physical one where you can. A slow breath out, a hand placed flat on the table, feet set on the floor: small acts that are easy to do in any room and that interrupt the momentum of a reading long enough for the plan to fire.

Test each trigger for a week before trusting it. A trigger you never notice is not a trigger.
teach.disconfirm: If your chosen internal signal turns out, over a fortnight, to arrive after you have already acted, it is too late to serve as a trigger. Look in your journal for an earlier signal in the same situations and try that instead.

teach.h: Compress six steps into three cues.
teach.p:
Attention narrows under stress, and working memory is small even at the best of times. Nelson Cowan's review of the evidence in 2001 put the number of separate items most people can hold in mind at once at around four. Six steps with several checks each will not survive a hard conversation. Three short cues might.

Aviation solved a version of this problem long ago. For most emergencies, pilots have a full written checklist. For the few where there is no time to read, they have memory items: a handful of actions learned by heart and done first, from memory, before the checklist comes out. The memory items do not replace the checklist. They hold the situation until the checklist can be used.

Your protocol needs the same split. The full six steps are for before and after: preparing for a conversation you know is coming, and writing up the journal entry that night. The memory items are for the moment itself. They should be three cues of a word or two each, chosen to cover the steps that matter most in the moment. One version that works for many people is *Me. Normal? Wrong if?*: check your own state, compare with this person's baseline, name what would prove the reading wrong.

Your three may differ. If your journal shows that your worst errors come from acting on a single striking signal, one cue might be *two channels?* If they come from your own temper, the first cue might be *breathe out*. Choose the cues from your record, not from this page.

Then say them silently, in order, until they arrive without effort.
teach.disconfirm: If your three cues reliably surface in hard moments but your readings in those moments are no better, the cues are covering the wrong steps. Compare your recent errors with the cues and swap the one that addresses the error least often.

teach.p:
In *The Checklist Manifesto* Atul Gawande described two kinds of checklist. With a read-do list you read each item and then do it. With a do-confirm list you do the work from memory and skill, then stop at a set point to confirm that nothing was missed. The surgical safety checklist he helped develop for the World Health Organization is built around pause points at which the whole team stops to confirm a few critical items, and when it was trialled in eight hospitals in eight countries, Alex Haynes and his colleagues reported in 2009 that deaths after surgery fell from about one and a half percent to under one percent, and complications from eleven percent to seven.

A reader's protocol can use both. Before a conversation you know matters, such as an appraisal, a difficult call with a parent, or a negotiation, run the full protocol as a read-do list. How am I, and what do I want from this? What is this person's baseline in settings like this? What am I most likely to misread, given my history with them? What will I ask rather than assume?

During the conversation, use only the memory items. Afterwards, run the protocol again as a do-confirm list. Did I check my own state? Did I compare with baseline, or with my mood? Did I name a rival before acting? Did I ask rather than trap? What would I record, and how sure was I?

The after-list does more than tidy up. It is where the protocol learns. Each confirmation is a small scored prediction about your own behaviour, and over a month the pattern of missed items shows you exactly which step fails under pressure.

Keep both lists short enough to fit on a single card.
teach.disconfirm: If running the full list before conversations makes you more anxious and your readings worse, cut it to two questions and see whether that helps. A checklist that raises your stress is undoing the first step of the protocol it serves.

teach.p:
The same six steps apply everywhere, but the risks are not the same everywhere, and a good protocol adjusts its emphasis to the setting. Keep one core and write a small variant for each part of your life where you read people often.

At work, power is the main risk. The variant might add a line about records, *behaviour only, nothing I wouldn't read aloud*, and raise the threshold for acting on any reading of someone you manage. At home, the main risk is reading too much. The variant might be mostly stopping rules: when the skill is off duty, and the reminder that the people you love most are the ones whose baselines you assume you know and therefore check least.

In negotiations or any setting where you want something, the main risk is your own stake. The variant might begin with *What do I want to be true?* and require a rival explanation for every encouraging signal as well as every discouraging one. In a culture or community you do not know well, which the next chapters take up, the variant leans on humility: no baseline yet, so start one, and ask people who know. In a crisis, where someone may be at risk, the variant is the shortest of all: safety first, ask directly, get help.

Each variant should change no more than one or two lines of the core. If a variant grows into a separate protocol, you will not remember which one you are meant to be running.

Name each variant after its setting, so that walking into that setting calls it up.
teach.disconfirm: If your ledger shows the same error rates and the same kinds of errors in every setting, variants are adding complexity without benefit. Keep the core alone, and revisit the question when the ledger shows a difference.

teach.p:
Treat your protocol like a piece of equipment that you maintain. Give it a version number and a date: *Protocol 1.0, March*. Change it only for reasons you can point to in the ledger, and record each change with its reason and its date.

The ledger shows two kinds of change worth making. The first is a step that never changes anything. If, over three months, a particular check has never altered a single reading or prediction, it may be a step you already do automatically, or one that does not apply to your life. Retire it, or reword it, and watch whether errors rise. The second is a cluster of errors. If your misses gather in one place, readings of senior colleagues, readings made when you are tired, readings of your son, add or sharpen a line aimed at that cluster, and nothing else.

Do not change the protocol often. New habits take time to settle. In 2010 Phillippa Lally and her colleagues followed people trying to make a new daily behaviour automatic and found that it took a median of about sixty-six days, with a range from under three weeks to well over half a year. The study was small and the longest estimates were extrapolated beyond its twelve weeks, but the lesson about variation stands. A protocol rewritten every fortnight never becomes a habit at all. A quarterly review is about right for most people.

Keep the old versions. Looking back from version four to version one shows you how your errors have changed, which is one of the clearest pictures of your progress that you will ever have.

The protocol is finished only when you stop reading people, which is to say never.
teach.disconfirm: If changes you make to the protocol in response to the ledger are followed, over the next quarter, by no change in the errors they targeted, your changes are aimed at the wrong cause. Look at the entries again, and ask what the misses have in common that your change did not touch.

caseStudy:
Martin, fifty-one, is a deputy head at a secondary school, and much of his week is spent in his office with pupils who have been sent out of lessons, and with their parents. He wrote his protocol after finishing Part I and was proud of it. Then, in October, a father arrived for a meeting about his son, folded his arms, and spoke loudly from the first sentence. Martin read aggression, felt his own voice rise to meet it, and within five minutes the meeting was over and the father was complaining to the head.

That evening, writing the journal entry, Martin saw that he had done none of his six steps. He had read the father's arms and volume in a single flash and answered them. So he wrote three if-then plans. *If a parent raises his voice, then I lower mine and put my hand flat on the desk.* *If I feel certain that someone is being difficult, then I ask one open question before I respond.* *If a pupil sits in silence, then I ask what happened, not why he did it.* He compressed the rest into three cues, *Hand. Normal? Ask.*, and tied the first to the handle of his office door.

For a month the plans fired about one time in three. He rehearsed them with a colleague playing an angry parent, which felt foolish and helped. By December they were firing most of the time.

In January a fourteen-year-old boy was sent to him after a fight and sat in silence, staring at the floor. Martin felt the familiar certainty, defiance, and his hand went to the desk before he had decided anything. He asked what had happened. After a long pause the boy said he was trying not to cry in front of a teacher. The fight had started when another boy said something about his father, who had left that week.

Martin's ledger for the term shows the silent-pupil plan firing eleven times. In nine of them, the silence was not defiance.
observe: Notice one moment this week when you knew what you meant to do in a tense moment and did something else, and what you felt just before it happened.
Notice the thresholds you cross every day, such as doorways, sitting down at a table or picking up the phone, that could serve as triggers for a self-check.
Notice the first sign in your own body that a conversation has become high-stakes for you, and how early it arrives.

drills.name: Three If-Thens
steps: Look through your journal for the three situations in which your readings most often turn into hasty actions.
For each situation, name a trigger you will notice when it happens: a place, a social moment, a time or an internal signal.
Write one if-then plan for each, with a single response that takes no more than a few seconds.
Read each plan aloud and change any word you would not naturally use.
Write the three plans on the first page of your ledger and mark each time one fires this week.
variations: Write one extra plan for the time of day when your journal shows most of your errors, and track it separately for a week.
Ask a friend who knows you well to read your three plans and tell you which situation they would have chosen instead.
After a week, rewrite any plan that fired fewer than three times with a trigger you are more likely to meet.

drills.name: Find Your Internal Trigger
steps: Choose five journal entries in which you misread someone and acted on the reading.
For each, write what you felt in your body in the seconds just before you acted.
Look for a sensation that appears in at least three of the five.
Choose a small physical act, such as a slow breath out or a hand flat on the table, to pair with that sensation.
Practise the pairing three times a day for a week by recalling one of the moments and doing the act.
variations: Repeat the drill with five entries in which a conversation went well, and compare what you felt before those with the misreadings.
Try three different physical acts over three weeks, one per week, and record which one you actually remember to do.
Ask someone you live with whether they can see the sensation from outside, such as a set jaw or a change in your breathing.

drills.name: Compress to Three
steps: Write out your full six-step protocol from Part I.
Mark the two or three steps whose absence caused most of your recent errors.
Turn each marked step into a cue of one or two words.
Say the three cues silently in order twenty times, spaced through the day.
Write them on a card, and after each tense conversation note whether they surfaced.
variations: Write two alternative sets of three cues, try each for a week, and keep the set that surfaced more often after tense conversations.
Record your cues aloud on your phone and listen to them on the way to a meeting you expect to be difficult.
Test your cues by recalling a hard conversation vividly for a minute, then checking whether all three came to mind.

drills.name: Pressure Rehearsal
steps: Ask a friend or colleague to play the other person in a mildly tense conversation you expect to have, such as a complaint or a refusal.
Agree on a signal for stopping, and keep the role-play to five minutes.
Run the conversation, using only your three cues and one if-then plan.
Stop and talk through which cues fired and which did not.
Run it a second time with your friend raising the pressure slightly, and note the difference.
variations: Run the rehearsal with the roles reversed, so that you feel what your usual habit is like from the other side.
Run it on a video call instead of in person, and notice which cues are harder to use on a screen.
Rehearse your crisis variant with your friend reading from a short script, keeping it calm and brief, and checking that you can say each step.

drills.name: Quarterly Version Review
steps: Gather your ledger, your after-lists and your journal entries for the past three months.
List any step that did not change a single reading or prediction in that time.
List the setting or kind of person where your errors cluster most.
Make at most two changes: retire or reword one step, and sharpen one line for the cluster.
Write the new version number, the date and the reason for each change at the top of the protocol.
variations: Before you change anything, ask a trusted friend to read your after-lists and tell you which step they think fails most often.
Compare your current version with your first one, and write a paragraph on how your errors have changed between them.
Make no changes at all this quarter, and write down why, if the ledger shows that the protocol is still settling.

quiz.q: You have written your protocol down and can recite it word for word. Will you use it in a tense moment?
options: Yes, because knowing it this well is exactly what makes you use it when it matters
Not reliably, because stress tends to push behaviour back towards old habits
Only if you have also read the research behind each of the six steps
Yes, as long as you keep a written copy close by at all times
quiz.explain: Knowledge is necessary and not sufficient. Under stress people slide back to their strongest habits, so the protocol has to be tied to triggers, compressed and rehearsed until it fires before the old habit does.

quiz.q: What is an implementation intention, in Peter Gollwitzer's sense?
options: A plan linking a specific situation to a specific response
A general goal stated clearly, such as I will read people more carefully
A promise made in front of another person, who will then hold you to account for it
A reminder on your phone to practise at the same time every day
quiz.explain: The if-then form hands control of the response to the situation, so you do not have to remember the goal and decide to act in the moment. Across ninety-four tests it had a medium-to-large effect on whether people followed through.

quiz.q: Why should the protocol have a short form of three cues for use in the moment itself?
options: Because the other three steps turn out not to matter very much in the end
Because short cues are easier to teach to other people than the full steps are
Because the full protocol is meant only for writing up journal entries
Because attention narrows under pressure, and only a few items can be held at once
quiz.explain: Working memory holds around four items even when calm, and stress narrows attention further. Like a pilot's memory items, the cues hold the situation; the full protocol is used before and after.

quiz.q: In a meeting you feel a sudden jolt of certainty that a colleague is hiding something from you. Which if-then plan fits this chapter?
options: If I feel certain, then I press him at once while the evidence is still fresh
If I feel certain, then I watch him more closely for the rest of the meeting
If I feel certain, then I name one rival explanation and ask one open question
If I feel certain, then I raise it with my manager after the meeting has ended
quiz.explain: The jolt of certainty is the moment a reading is about to turn into an action, which is exactly where a plan belongs. Naming a rival and asking openly runs the core of the protocol in a few seconds.

quiz.q: In Phillippa Lally's study of habit formation, how long did a new daily behaviour take to become automatic?
options: A median of about sixty-six days, varying widely between people
Exactly twenty-one days for almost everyone who took part in it
About a week, provided the behaviour was repeated every single day
More than a year in every case, however simple the behaviour was
quiz.explain: The median was around sixty-six days, with a range from under three weeks to well over half a year. That is why a protocol rewritten every fortnight never becomes a habit, and why a quarterly review suits most people.

quiz.q: Your ledger shows that one step of your protocol has not changed a single reading in three months. What fits this chapter?
options: Keep it as it is, since every step was put there for a good reason
Throw out the whole protocol and write a new one from scratch
Retire or reword the step, date the new version, and watch whether errors rise
Add two more steps alongside it to make up for the one that is not working
quiz.explain: A step that never changes anything is either already automatic or does not apply to your life. Retire or reword it, record the change and its reason, and let the next quarter's ledger show whether it mattered.

quiz.q: What did Schwabe and Wolf find in 2009 when they stressed people after training them to win rewards?
options: Stressed people adapted to the new reward values faster than those who had not been stressed
Stress made no difference at all, since everyone adapted to the new reward values at much the same speed
Stressed people kept making the old, now pointless responses more than those who were not stressed
Stressed people refused to take part in the second half of the task and left before it ended
quiz.explain: Stress shifted people from acting on goals towards acting on habit. It is why a protocol known by heart can still fail in a tense moment, unless it has become the habit or is tied firmly to the situation.

quiz.q: Your if-then plan says *When things get tense, I will slow down*. After three months it has never fired. What is the best change?
options: Replace the trigger with something specific you will notice, such as a phrase you say or a sensation
Add more plans for other moods, so that at least one of them is bound to fire before long
Read the plan aloud every morning, so that it is fresh in your mind when things do get tense
Give up on if-then plans and rely on your judgement, since plans clearly do not suit the way you work
quiz.explain: *When things get tense* is a mood, not a moment you can notice, so the plan has nothing to fire on. A trigger must reliably occur, be noticeable and arrive early enough for the response to matter.

quiz.q: Someone says people can hold about seven things in mind at once, so a six-step protocol will be fine in a hard conversation. What does the chapter say?
options: That Cowan's review found most people can hold a dozen items, so the protocol could even be longer
That memory is irrelevant, since the steps of the protocol are written down on a card in your pocket
That anyone who has read the protocol often enough will remember all six steps under any pressure
That Cowan's review put the number at around four, which is why the moment itself needs three cues
quiz.explain: Working memory is small even at the best of times, and attention narrows under stress. The full protocol belongs before and after the conversation; three short cues are what survive during it.

reflection.prompt: Describe one specific situation that comes round regularly in your life, such as a weekly meeting, a phone call with a parent or the moment you get home, in which you often misread someone or react before you think. What is the first sign, in the room or in your own body, that this situation has begun? Write one if-then plan tied to that sign, and say how you will know in a fortnight whether it has fired.
reflection.guidance: The situation should be one that actually recurs, so that you can practise on it. Most people find the first sign is either a place, such as the front door, or a sensation, such as heat in the face. The plan should fit in one sentence and take a few seconds to carry out. Count the times it fires, and the times it should have and did not.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to build a beautiful protocol that never runs: pages of steps, colour-coded variants, and a man who still answers raised voices with his own. The second is constant tinkering, a new version every week, so that nothing ever becomes habit. The third is vague triggers, *when things get tense*, which never fire because they never arrive at a moment you can notice. A subtler failure is mechanical use. A protocol run at a grieving friend, or used to make a biased reaction sound rational afterwards, has stopped serving its purpose. The protocol exists to make you slower to judge and quicker to ask. If it ever makes you colder, put it down and use the stopping rules instead.

moreCases.title: The receptionist whose trigger never fired
moreCases.scene:
Sarah, thirty-seven, works on the front desk of a busy GP surgery, where much of her day is spent with people who are worried, unwell or frustrated by the wait for an appointment. After Part I she wrote a plan for the hardest moments: *When things get tense, I'll slow down and listen.* She liked it. It sounded calm and kind.

Three months later she reads back through her journal and finds that the plan has never once fired. On the worst days she remembers it afterwards, on the bus home, but never in the moment. There was no point at which things *got tense*; they were simply tense, and she was already answering.

So she goes back through the entries where an exchange at the desk went badly, looking for what happened in her own body and speech just before. The pattern surprises her. In almost every one, there is a moment when she hears herself say *I'm afraid the policy is*, and a moment just before that when her neck goes hot. In the exchanges that went well, she never said it at all.

She writes a new plan: *If I hear myself start to say "the policy is", then I stop and ask what they need today.*

She had also noticed that she said it faster each time, as if getting the words out quickly would make the conversation end sooner.
moreCases.misread:
Sarah read her first plan as a good one because its intention was good. But *when things get tense* is a mood, not a moment, and a mood arrives without a moment you can notice. The plan had no trigger, so it could never fire.

She had also read her own forgetting as a lack of willpower, and had resolved each evening to try harder, which changed nothing.

Her manager had praised the plan when she showed it to him, which had made it feel finished.
moreCases.betterRead:
A trigger has to be something that reliably happens, that you will notice when it happens, and that arrives early enough for the response to matter. Sarah's journal found her one that met all three: a phrase she used only when an exchange was going wrong, preceded by a sensation she could learn to catch. The new plan fired on its second day. A man shouting about a repeat prescription heard, instead of the policy, *What do you need today?* He needed his blood-pressure tablets before the weekend, and there was a way to get them that Sarah had not thought of while she was defending the rules.

She also noticed that the hot neck came first, a second or two before the phrase, and began to use that as an earlier trigger.

Over the next month she caught the hot neck before the phrase about half the time, and the phrase itself almost every time. Her journal for that month has fewer entries about the desk, because fewer exchanges went badly enough to write about.

moreCases.title: The father who brought his work protocol home
moreCases.scene:
Gareth, forty-five, is an operations manager who has used this book's method at work for a year, with good results. His one-to-ones with his team are calmer, and his ledger shows his predictions about meetings improving steadily. Pleased, he starts running the same protocol at home.

At dinner he checks his own state, notes his wife's baseline, and watches his daughter, Erin, fifteen, for changes from hers. When Erin goes quiet after a phone call, he asks, gently, whether the call has upset her, and mentions that her shoulders went up when she read the message. When his wife sighs at the washing-up, he asks whether something is on her mind, since she has been quieter than usual since Tuesday.

After a fortnight Erin tells him, at the table, to stop doing *the face thing*. He asks what she means. She says that he watches everybody now, like a teacher during an exam, and that it is creepy. His wife says nothing, but later tells him that she has started to feel as if she is being assessed in her own kitchen.

Gareth is hurt. He had thought he was paying more attention to his family, which is what he has always been told good fathers do.

He had even started writing short notes about the family in his ledger, the same way he did for work, and had told himself it was practice.
moreCases.misread:
Gareth read his family's discomfort as a misunderstanding of his motives, and read his close watching as care. They read it as being assessed, which is what it was. The protocol was built for work, where the main risk is power, and at home it went looking for things to read.

He also read his wife's silence, after Erin's remark, as agreement with him rather than with her daughter.
moreCases.betterRead:
The chapter's point about variants applies exactly. At home the main risk is reading too much, so the home variant should be mostly stopping rules, and Gareth's had none. He wrote one: the skill is off duty at meals and in the car, he never announces a reading of anyone in the family, and when he is worried he asks an open question without saying what prompted it. He also told Erin she was right, which surprised her. A month later she mentioned, unprompted, that a friend was having a hard time and asked him what she should say, which she had not done for a long while.

Gareth kept his ledger for work only.

He found the change harder than any he had made at work. Reading his family had felt like love, and stopping felt like caring less. His wife told him, some weeks later, that it felt like the opposite.

moreCases.title: The buyer who rewrote her protocol every week
moreCases.scene:
Leila, thirty-eight, manages purchasing for a chain of garden centres and spends much of her week negotiating with suppliers. She took to the protocol chapter with energy. Her first version, 1.0, had six steps and two if-then plans. Within a week she had found a better phrasing for the second plan and called it 1.1. Then she added a negotiation variant, then a variant for phone calls, then a colour code for the strength of each signal.

After two months she is on version 3.7. The protocol runs to four pages and she is proud of it. It is, by any standard, a thoughtful document.

But her ledger tells a different story. Her if-then plans, as far as she can tell, fire in perhaps one negotiation in five. When she tries to remember her three cues in the middle of a hard conversation, she is not sure which version's cues she is meant to be using. Twice she has caught herself, mid-meeting, trying to recall whether she had moved *Wrong if?* to the front or the back.

A colleague asks her which version worked best. Leila realises she cannot say, because none of them was used for long enough to find out.

Her negotiation variant alone has eleven steps, and the latest version has a footnote explaining why one of them was moved.
moreCases.misread:
Leila read each improvement as progress, because each version was better written than the last. But a protocol rewritten every week never becomes a habit, and the moments that need it are the moments when only habits are available.

She read her uncertainty about which cues to use, in the middle of meetings, as a sign that the protocol still needed work, rather than as a sign that it needed leaving alone.
moreCases.betterRead:
Lally's study is the useful benchmark here: a new daily behaviour took a median of about sixty-six days to become automatic, with wide variation between people. A protocol changed weekly never gets the chance. Leila went back to a version close to 1.0, with three cues and two plans, and froze it for a quarter. She kept a page of ideas for changes, but made none of them until the review date. By the end of the quarter her plans were firing in most negotiations, and the page of ideas had shrunk, because most of the changes she had wanted turned out not to be needed.

At the review, she made one change, and it was one she had first written down in the second week.

She also noticed that her colleagues had started asking her for advice on negotiations, which they had not done while her protocol ran to four pages.

moreCases.title: The interviewer whose protocol came afterwards
moreCases.scene:
Neil, forty-nine, is a hiring manager at a logistics firm, and he sits on interview panels most weeks. He has a protocol and is careful to use it. After each interview he writes a short note on each candidate, structured by its steps.

One afternoon the panel interviews Tomasz, thirty-three, for a senior planning role. Tomasz speaks fluent English with a strong accent, has a fairly still face, and often looks away to the side before answering harder questions. Neil comes out of the interview with a firm sense that he was evasive. His note reads: *Two channels: gaze aversion on hard questions, short answers. Rival considered: nerves. Ruled out, as he was calm elsewhere. Concern about candour.*

Abi, forty, who sat on the same panel, reads the note and asks to talk. She points out that the short answers were complete answers to closed questions, and that when the panel asked open ones, Tomasz gave the most detailed answers of the day. She adds that many people look away while they think about a hard question, and that she does it herself. She asks Neil when, exactly, he ruled out nerves, and how.

Neil realises that he cannot say. He wrote the rival down and crossed it out in the same sentence.

The two other candidates interviewed that afternoon, both of whom Neil had liked, had given shorter answers to the open questions than Tomasz had.
moreCases.misread:
Neil read his own note as a careful reading, because it used the protocol's steps. It was a gut reaction written up in the protocol's language afterwards. Looking away while thinking, a still face and an accent were read as evasion, and the rival was dismissed rather than tested.

He also read the still face as a lack of warmth, without any baseline for how Tomasz's face looked when he was relaxed.
moreCases.betterRead:
This is the subtler failure the chapter warns about: a protocol used to make a biased reaction sound rational. The steps have value only if they are run before the conclusion, and a rival is considered only when something could have ruled it in. Neil's fix was partly personal and partly structural. He added a line to his interview variant, *What do I want to be true, and what would change my mind?*, to be answered before he formed a view. He also asked the firm to score every candidate's answers to the same questions against the job, separately, before the panel discussed anyone, so that impressions of manner came last. Tomasz was offered the job.

Neil also asked Abi to keep asking him how he knew, which she did, cheerfully, at every panel for the rest of the year.

Abi said afterwards that the note had been useful, because it made the reasoning visible enough to question. A gut feeling that had never been written down could not have been challenged at all.

workedReading.title: One appraisal, before, during and after
workedReading.scene:
Hana, forty-two, leads a team of eight in a housing association, and has an appraisal tomorrow with Owen, twenty-nine, whose work has slipped over the past two months: missed deadlines, two complaints from tenants about slow replies, and less in team meetings than usual. She expects the meeting to be awkward, and she has a prediction in her ledger: *Owen will be defensive about the deadlines, 70%.* She has a full protocol, a work variant, three cues that have become habit over the spring, and two if-then plans. She has decided to run the whole sequence properly: the read-do list the evening before, only the memory items in the room, and the do-confirm list afterwards.

She has also written down, as she was taught, the one thing she will not do: decide what the problem is before Owen has said anything.

She has run this sequence a dozen times since the spring, and it no longer feels like a performance.

steps.label: Read-do the night before
steps.text:
The evening before, Hana sits down with the card and runs the full protocol as a read-do list. *How am I?* Tired, and slightly irritated with Owen, which she writes down because it will colour what she sees. *What is his baseline in settings like this?* In last year's appraisal he was chatty and asked lots of questions. *What am I most likely to misread?* Quietness as sulking, since that is her old habit with junior staff. *What will I ask rather than assume?* Whether something has changed for him.

She writes her answers in a few lines, and notices that the process has already softened her irritation a little, simply by naming it.

steps.label: Name what she wants
steps.text:
Her work variant adds one line: *What do I want to be true?* She answers it honestly. She wants Owen to be at fault in a simple way, because that would be quick to fix and would mean her own management had not missed anything. She notes that this makes her more likely to read his behaviour as attitude rather than as a sign of something else, and decides to look for one reading that would make her own management part of the story.

The answer she finds is that she has not had a proper one-to-one with Owen since the spring, when the team was short-staffed.

steps.label: The doorway trigger
steps.text:
In the morning she walks to the meeting room, and her hand on the door handle sets off the first if-then plan, which has been tied to that handle for months: *breathe out, feet on the floor*. She does it before she goes in. It takes two seconds. Owen is already there, and she sits at the corner of the table rather than opposite him, which is something her variant suggests for conversations that might feel like a judgement.

She also puts her phone face down and out of reach, which is part of the same plan.

steps.label: Memory items in the room
steps.text:
In the meeting she uses only her three cues, *Me. Normal? Ask.* She starts with the things that have gone well, and Owen is subdued but polite. When she reaches the deadlines, he goes quiet, looks down at the table and holds the edge of his notebook. *Normal?* He was never like this last year. That is a change from his baseline, in at least two channels, at a clear moment: the mention of deadlines.

She does not think about the full protocol at all. The cues are enough to hold the moment.

Owen's quietness is not, by itself, a reading of anything. It is a change, and the cues have only told her where to look.

steps.label: The jolt, and a rival
steps.text:
Hana feels the jolt of certainty she has learned to treat as a trigger: *he doesn't care, and he's sulking*. Her second plan fires: *If I feel sure what someone is thinking, then I name one rival before I speak.* She names it silently: *he's embarrassed, or something is going on outside work.* Then *Ask.* She says, *You've seemed under pressure lately. Has anything changed for you?* After a long pause, Owen tells her that his mother had an operation in the spring and that he has been looking after her in the evenings, then working late into the night to catch up.

She thanks him for telling her, and they spend the rest of the meeting on what would help, rather than on the deadlines themselves.

steps.label: Do-confirm afterwards
steps.text:
That evening she runs the do-confirm list. Did she check her own state? Yes, at the door. Did she compare with Owen's baseline, or with her mood? Mostly baseline, though she notices that her prediction had been based on her irritation, not on him. Did she name a rival before acting? Yes. Did she ask rather than trap? Yes. What would she record? Behaviour only: *quiet and looking down when deadlines raised; disclosed caring responsibilities; agreed changes.* How sure was she? Her ledger prediction was 70% defensive, and it was wrong.

She also records something she had nearly missed: that her own lack of one-to-ones over the spring was part of why nobody had known.

steps.label: What the after-list showed
steps.text:
Over the following month Hana runs the after-list after every important conversation. The pattern is clear by the fourth week. Her cues fire reliably, and her rivals are good when she names them. The step that fails most is the one she had thought was her strongest: the comparison with baseline, which she keeps replacing, without noticing, with her expectations. At the next quarterly review that is the one line she changes. Owen's deadlines recover within six weeks, once they agree he can start and finish an hour earlier.

She also adds a monthly one-to-one with each member of her team to her calendar, which is not part of the protocol but came out of it.

moreFailures.title: Writing plans for situations you rarely meet
moreFailures.body:
It is tempting to write if-then plans for the dramatic moments: the furious customer, the colleague in tears, the stranger who seems to be in trouble. Those moments matter, but they are rare, and a plan that fires twice a year never gets the practice it needs to be there when it is wanted. The plans that change most are those attached to situations you meet every day or every week: walking into meetings, answering the phone, sitting down to dinner, the jolt of certainty that comes several times a day. Each firing is a repetition, and repetitions are what turn a plan into a habit. Start with frequent triggers. Once those plans fire without effort, the habit of pausing they build will help in the rare moments too, and for the rarest and most serious, such as a crisis, a plan can be rehearsed deliberately.

A useful check is to count how many times each plan fired last week. If the answer is zero for any of them, change the trigger before you change anything else.

moreFailures.title: Responses you cannot do on purpose
moreFailures.body:
Many plans fail at the *then*. *If someone raises their voice, then I stay calm.* *If I feel certain, then I keep an open mind.* Staying calm and keeping an open mind are states, not actions, and you cannot produce a state on demand, least of all under stress. The plan fires, you remember it, and nothing happens, because there was nothing to do. Write responses that are actions you can take in a few seconds whatever you are feeling: breathe out slowly, put a hand flat on the table, lower your voice, name one rival silently, ask one open question. The actions often bring the state with them, a little later. Even when they do not, they have interrupted the habit long enough for the rest of the protocol to have a chance.

Test a response by asking whether you could do it while furious. If not, it is a hope rather than an action.

Write the response as something a person watching you could see you do. If they could not, rewrite it.

moreFailures.title: Skipping the after-list when things went well
moreFailures.body:
The do-confirm list is easy to run after a conversation that went badly, because you want to know what went wrong. It is easy to skip after one that went well, because there seems to be nothing to learn. Over a few months that bias distorts the record. The ledger fills with disasters, the protocol is tuned to prevent them, and you never discover which steps were doing the work in the good conversations, or that a conversation went well despite a step you skipped. Run the after-list after every conversation that mattered, whatever its outcome, and keep it short enough that doing so is no burden. A good outcome reached by luck is the most important thing the list can catch, because it is the one you would otherwise repeat.

Over a quarter, the after-lists from good conversations are often the ones that show you which steps to keep.

A quick version is enough for routine conversations: one line for each item, written within an hour.

moreFailures.title: Borrowing someone else's protocol
moreFailures.body:
A colleague's cues, or the examples in this chapter, can look so neat that it seems easier to adopt them than to build your own. *Me. Normal? Wrong if?* works for many people, but it was chosen to cover common errors, not yours. If your own journal shows that your worst misreadings come from your temper, a cue about baselines will not catch them; if they come from acting on a single striking signal, a cue about your own state will not help either. A borrowed protocol also fails at the trigger, because the internal signals that matter most are personal. One person's warning sign is heat in the face, another's is the sudden wish to be clever. Use other people's protocols as examples of form. Fill the form from your own record.

The same applies to this book. Its examples are there to show what a protocol looks like. Yours should look like your mistakes.

Borrowing is also how folk wisdom spreads. A neat cue repeated by enough people starts to sound like research, and nobody remembers that it began as one person's guess about their own mistakes.

questions.q: How can I rehearse a plan for a situation that I cannot easily set up, such as a crisis?
questions.a:
In two ways. First, mental rehearsal: imagine the situation as specifically as you can, where you are, who is there and what you notice first, and then imagine doing the response, in your own words, all the way through. It feels artificial, but it gives the plan a first use before it is needed. Second, role-play with someone you trust, keeping it brief and agreeing a signal to stop. For a crisis, where someone may be at risk, keep the plan very short and the same every time: safety first, ask directly, get help. Know in advance how you would get help where you live, including the numbers in this app's crisis resources, so that you do not have to look for them while someone needs you.

Rehearse the crisis variant every few months, not just once, because a plan you never use fades.

questions.q: What should I do if an if-then plan fires at the wrong moments, or far too often?
questions.a:
Narrow the trigger. A plan tied to *someone raises their voice* will fire at a football match, in a noisy pub and when your mother is calling from the garden, and after a while you will start ignoring it, which teaches you to ignore it when it matters. Add the setting or the person: *If someone raises their voice at me at work*, or *in a meeting I am chairing*. Alternatively, choose a different trigger closer to the moment you care about, such as an internal signal that comes only when you are about to misread. A plan that fires a few times a day in the right situations is more useful than one that fires constantly.

If a plan fires rarely in the right situations and often in the wrong ones, the trigger is probably a common sensation rather than the specific one that precedes your mistakes. Look again in the journal.

questions.q: Should I tell people that I am using a protocol when I talk to them?
questions.a:
You do not need to announce it, any more than a doctor announces each item on a checklist. But if someone asks why you paused, or why you asked a question instead of answering, tell them honestly. At work, sharing the parts of the protocol that are about asking rather than assuming can help: a team that knows you will check before you judge may find it easier to tell you things directly. What you should not do is present it as a method for reading people's hidden thoughts. It is a method for slowing yourself down, and describing it that way is both more accurate and less alarming for the people around you.

If someone you are with asks directly whether you are reading them, tell the truth, and stop if they would rather you did not.

It also helps to be clear with yourself about the difference. The protocol is a set of habits for your own behaviour. It does not give you access to anyone else's mind, and talking about it as if it did would mislead you as much as anyone else.

questions.q: My three cues stop working when I am very angry. Is there anything shorter that will still work?
questions.a:
Yes: a single physical act, rehearsed until it is automatic. A slow breath out, a hand flat on the table or your feet set on the floor will still be available when words are not, and they buy the second or two in which the cues can return. If you are too angry even for that, use a stopping rule rather than a reading rule. Say something you have prepared in advance, such as *Let me think about that and come back to you*, and leave the conversation until you can run the protocol properly. No reading made at the height of anger is worth acting on, and the most useful thing a protocol can do in that state is get you out of the room.

Afterwards, when you are calm, write the moment in your journal. Anger is one of the most useful triggers to learn from, because it is so reliable.

questions.q: Can the protocol still help me if I have always found faces hard to read?
questions.a:
Yes, and perhaps more than it helps others. Most of the protocol is not about reading faces at all. It is about checking your own state, comparing with what is normal for this person, naming a rival explanation and asking rather than assuming. None of that depends on reading expressions well. If faces are hard for you, lean on the channels you read better, such as voice, timing or what people do, and lean especially on asking. Your variant might put *Ask* first rather than last. People who find faces hard often become very good at checking directly, which is the step most confident readers skip.

If you find faces hard, you may also be less likely than others to feel the false certainty that a single expression produces, which is one of the commonest sources of error in this book.

The same is true of the other end of the protocol. A journal and a ledger work just as well for someone who reads faces poorly, and will show you which of your other channels you can trust.

questions.q: How many variants should my protocol have?
questions.a:
Usually two or three, one for each part of your life where you read people often and where the risks are different, such as work, home and one other setting that matters to you, like negotiations or volunteering. Each should change no more than one or two lines of the core. If you find yourself writing a fourth or fifth, check whether the settings really differ in their risks, or whether you are writing variants instead of practising the core. The crisis variant is the exception: it should exist for everyone, and it should be the shortest of all.

Write each variant on the back of the card that holds the core, so that you can see at a glance how little it changes.

Review the variants at the same quarterly review as the core, and retire any you have not used in the past three months.

watch.title: The Checklist Manifesto
watch.notice: Atul Gawande on how simple checklists improved surgical outcomes. Listen for why experts resist them, and why a short written procedure works under pressure.

reviewPrompt: Write one if-then plan tied to a trigger you will meet this week, and count the times it fires.
